area: Area IV. Flight by Reference to Instruments
objective: By the end of this lesson you can fly straight and level, climbs, descents and standard-rate turns by instruments alone, using a smooth cross-check and the right pitch, bank, power and trim corrections, with a full or partial panel.
why: Every instrument approach, departure and en route leg is built from these basic maneuvers. When the clouds close in, a failed gyro or your own inner ear can turn a routine flight into a loss of control unless your scan and corrections are automatic.

prereading.label: IFH Ch 6, 6-1 to 6-13

prereading.what: The four-step process, scanning a glass display (PFD), trend vectors, and fixation, omission and emphasis on glass.
prereading.label: IFH Ch 6, 6-19 to 6-28

prereading.what: Straight-and-level flight, airspeed changes, trim, climbs, descents, level-offs, standard-rate, timed and compass turns, and the common errors lists.
prereading.label: IFH Ch 7, 7-1 to 7-26

prereading.label: IFH 7-36 to 7-37

prereading.label: IFH 5-2 to 5-3

prereading.what: Gyro power sources, attitude indicator, heading indicator, turn-and-slip indicator and turn coordinator.
prereading.label: IFH 5-17 to 5-21

warmup: You are in the clouds and the attitude indicator shows wings level, but the heading indicator is slowly turning and the altimeter is creeping down. Which instrument do you believe, and how would you find out?

key_terms.def: Controlling the airplane's pitch and bank by reference to instruments instead of the outside horizon.
The attitude indicator and power indicators. You set attitude and power on these.
Altimeter, airspeed indicator and VSI. They show what the airplane is actually doing.
The instrument that gives the most useful information for a maneuver, usually the one you hold constant.
An instrument that helps you keep the primary one where you want it, often by showing a trend early.
The continuous, logical look at the instruments for attitude and performance information.
Staring at one instrument while the others drift.
Leaving an instrument out of the cross-check.
Relying on one instrument instead of the combination of instruments you need.
A turn of 3° per second: a full 360° in 2 minutes.
Flying with the attitude indicator and heading indicator failed or covered.
Not knowing the airplane's position, attitude or movement, often from false inner-ear sensations in clouds.

chunks.title: Control and performance: attitude plus power equals performance

body.p: In instrument flight you control attitude by the flight instruments instead of the natural horizon. Read correctly, they give you the same information the outside view gives you in visual flight [[23:135|IFH 6-2]].
The control and performance method sorts the panel into three groups [[23:135|IFH 6-2]]:

head: Group
Instruments
What they tell you
rows: Attitude indicator and power indicators (manifold pressure, tachometer, fuel flow) [[23:135|IFH 6-2]]
Attitude and power, right now. You set these.
What the airplane is actually doing
Course indicators, range indicators, glideslope, bearing pointers [[23:135|IFH 6-2]]
Where you are relative to a facility or fix

callout.text: Four steps: Establish, Trim, Cross-check, Adjust [[23:152|IFH 6-19]].

bullets: Establish: set attitude and power on the control instruments. Knowing approximate pitch and power settings cuts your workload [[23:135|IFH 6-2]].
Trim until the control pressures are gone. Hands-off trim lets you do other cockpit work without drifting [[23:135|IFH 6-2]] [[23:136|IFH 6-3]].
Cross-check the performance instruments. See and interpret: how big is the error, and which way [[23:136|IFH 6-3]]?
Adjust attitude or power on the control instruments, in small steps [[23:136|IFH 6-3]] [[23:153|IFH 6-20]].

body.p: The same picture gives different results in different airplanes. Full power and two bar widths nose-up gives a small airplane 500 fpm at 90 knots. The same attitude in a jet gives 2,000 fpm at 250 knots [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].

callout.text: Poor trim is one of the most common errors instructors see in instrument students. Another is making a bigger change than needed when you spot a deviation [[23:153|IFH 6-20]].

check.q: In the control and performance method, which instruments do you set, and which do you check?
check.a: You set the control instruments (attitude indicator and power indicators). You check the performance instruments (altimeter, airspeed, VSI) [[23:135|IFH 6-2]].

body.p: The primary and supporting method groups the instruments by what they control: pitch, bank, power and trim [[23:137|IFH 6-4]]. The primary instrument is the one that gives the most pertinent information for the maneuver. It is usually the one you want to hold constant [[23:167|IFH 7-6]]. The rest are supporting instruments.

head: Maneuver
Primary pitch
Primary bank
Primary power
rows: Manifold pressure while you change power, then airspeed again [[23:172|IFH 7-11]]
Turn coordinator once the turn is set up

body.p: The attitude indicator is the only instrument that shows pitch and bank instantly and directly. The primary and supporting idea never lowers its value: use it whenever you have it [[23:143|IFH 6-10]]. Whichever instrument tells you a pitch change is needed, make the change on the attitude indicator [[23:140|IFH 6-7]].

callout.text: Primary is a teaching tool, not a law. A proficient pilot in a slower airplane may lean on the altimeter for pitch; in a fast airplane, changes must be caught instantly. The IFH normally treats the altimeter as primary pitch in level flight [[23:167|IFH 7-6]].

check.q: You are in a stabilized constant-airspeed climb. Which instrument is primary for pitch?
check.a: The airspeed indicator. If the airspeed is low or high, make a small pitch correction [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].

body.p: Two skills make attitude instrument flying work: cross-check and instrument interpretation [[23:143|IFH 6-10]]. Cross-checking is the continuous, logical look at the instruments. No one method is required. Use the instruments that give the best information for the maneuver you are flying [[23:143|IFH 6-10]].

head: Pattern
How it works
rows: Eyes on the attitude indicator 80 to 90 percent of the time. Quick glances out to another instrument and back. Your eyes never go straight from one instrument to another [[23:144|IFH 6-11]]
Attitude indicator, down to the turn coordinator, back up, down to the VSI, back up [[23:144|IFH 6-11]]
Across the top row, then the bottom row. Every instrument gets equal weight, so it takes longer to get back to the critical one [[23:144|IFH 6-11]]

body.p: **On a glass display (PFD)** the attitude indicator spans the screen, so it stays in your side vision. Start on the yellow chevron. Go left to airspeed and back to center, right to altitude and back, up to the roll pointer and slip/skid indicator and back, then down to heading and back [[23:157|IFH 6-24]] [[23:158|IFH 6-25]].

Trend vectors on the airspeed, altitude and turn-rate displays show where that value will be in a few seconds if the present rate holds. The time depends on the system: 6 seconds on one IFH example, 10 on another [[23:159|IFH 6-26]]. Use them as a supplement, not as your main pitch reference [[23:160|IFH 6-27]].
**Interpretation** starts with knowing how each instrument works. Then you apply it to this airplane, this maneuver and today's conditions [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].

callout.text: Include the engine instruments and the standby instruments in your scan, even on a glass panel. At no time should you stop cross-checking [[23:157|IFH 6-24]].

check.q: With a radial cross-check, how do your eyes get from the altimeter to the heading indicator?
check.a: Through the attitude indicator. In the radial scan, the eyes never travel directly between the other flight instruments [[23:144|IFH 6-11]].

body.p: A beginner may scan fast without knowing what to look for. With practice you learn what to look for, when, and what to do about it [[23:144|IFH 6-11]]. Three errors break the cross-check:

head: Error
What it is
IFH example
rows: Staring at an altimeter 200 ft low while tension on the yoke lets the heading wander [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. On glass: staring at a trend vector, or trying to hold airspeed to 1 knot [[23:160|IFH 6-27]] [[23:161|IFH 6-28]]
Leaving an instrument out of the scan

Rolling out of a 180° steep turn on the attitude indicator alone and missing a heading change the precessed gyro hides [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. On glass: the standby instruments, compass and slip/skid indicator [[23:161|IFH 6-28]]
Relying on one instrument instead of the combination
Holding altitude on the attitude indicator alone: close, but not precise without the altimeter [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]

body.p: Turns invite fixation. Once you set up a standard-rate turn for a 90° heading change, the heading indicator can leave your scan for about 20 seconds, because the turn won't reach the lead point before then. Spend that time on pitch, power and trim [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

callout.text: Fixation = staring. Omission = skipping. Emphasis = trusting just one.

check.q: During an airspeed change you keep staring at the manifold pressure gauge and drift 150 ft high. Which error is this?
check.a: Fixation. The airplane will not slow down any faster because you stare at the gauge, and a small power error matters less than large altitude and heading errors [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].

chunks.title: Pitch, bank and power instruments: what they show and their limits

body.p: Each instrument tells part of the story. Know what it shows, how quickly, and where it can fool you.

head: Instrument
What it shows
Limits and traps
rows: Pitch and bank, directly and instantly [[23:140|IFH 6-7]]. The symbolic airplane's wings are about 2° of pitch wide [[23:114|IFH 5-19]]
Older types tumble past about 60° of pitch or 100° of roll. Small errors after a fast speed change or a 180° turn, which fix themselves within about a minute [[23:114|IFH 5-19]]
The only instrument with exact altitude; an indirect pitch reference in level flight at constant power [[23:140|IFH 6-7]] [[23:164|IFH 7-3]]
Not a good pitch reference in very strong vertical currents, like thunderstorms [[23:140|IFH 6-7]]
First a trend, then a rate [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]
Lags after a pitch change. A big, abrupt change makes the lag worse and can show a reverse reading. Don't chase it in turbulence [[23:166|IFH 7-5]]. An IVSI has little or no lag [[23:139|IFH 6-6]]
Indirect pitch reference; primary for power in level flight [[23:167|IFH 7-6]] [[23:143|IFH 6-10]]
Its apparent lag comes from the airplane speeding up or slowing down, not from the instrument [[23:166|IFH 7-5]]
Primary for bank in straight flight. Fast card movement means a big bank [[23:168|IFH 7-7]]
Not north-seeking. Compare it with the compass at least every 15 minutes [[23:115|IFH 5-20]]
Roll rate, then rate of turn. On the mark, 3° per second [[23:168|IFH 7-7]]
Once the roll stops it shows only direction and rate of turn. Don't assume a bank unless the ball is centered [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Quality of the turn: centered means coordinated [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]
Off center means a slip or skid [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]
Heading, with no outside power needed [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]
Affected by acceleration, turbulence, climbs, descents and power changes; leads and lags in turns [[23:140|IFH 6-7]]
Not affected by turbulence, bad trim or stray control pressure, so a quick glance is enough [[23:137|IFH 6-4]]

body.p: Ball to the left with the left wing low is a slip: add left rudder to center the ball and use aileron to level the wings. Wings level with the ball off center is a skid. Use the same fix: center the ball with rudder on the ball's side, then retrim [[23:169|IFH 7-8]].

check.q: The turn coordinator's miniature airplane sits on the standard-rate mark after the roll has stopped. What does that tell you?
check.a: You are turning 3° per second, 360° in 2 minutes [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]. It shows rate of turn, not bank angle [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].

body.p: At a constant airspeed there is only one pitch attitude for level flight. It is nose-high at slow cruise and nose-low at fast cruise [[23:163|IFH 7-2]]. After you level off at normal cruise, adjust the attitude indicator's miniature airplane to show level flight [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].
**Pitch**

bullets: Relax your grip. Make small, smooth pitch changes, and learn to hold half, one, and one-and-a-half bar widths [[23:164|IFH 7-3]].
Altitude error under 100 ft: half a bar width. Over 100 ft: start with a full bar width [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]. On a PFD, try about 1° of pitch for errors under 100 ft [[23:197|IFH 7-36]].
Correct in two steps: first stop the needle, then return to the altitude [[23:165|IFH 7-4]].
Use a VSI rate about double the error: 100 ft off, 200 fpm [[23:166|IFH 7-5]]. More than 200 fpm past that rate is overcontrolling [[23:139|IFH 6-6]] [[23:198|IFH 7-37]].
While you return to an altitude, the VSI is primary for pitch [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].

body.p: **Bank.** Fix a heading error with a bank no bigger than the number of degrees to turn, and never more than a standard-rate bank [[23:168|IFH 7-7]]. Correcting a 10° error with 20° of bank overshoots [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].
**Pitch or power?** Think of altitude and airspeed as interchangeable [[23:169|IFH 7-8]].

head: You see
Fix
rows: Altitude high and airspeed low, or the reverse
Altitude and airspeed both high, or both low
Check the altimeter first, then decide on power [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]

callout.text: IFH example, slowing from 120 to 100 knots: drop from 23 to about 15 inches (underpower), raise the nose as you slow to hold altitude, be ready with rudder, trim, then set about 18 inches as the airspeed nears 100 knots [[23:170|IFH 7-9]] [[23:172|IFH 7-11]].

body.p: **Trim.** Set the attitude with control pressure, then trim the pressure away. Using trim alone to change attitude leads to erratic control [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]. Use rudder trim toward the side the ball is displaced [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

check.q: You are 60 ft high in level cruise. About how much pitch change, and what VSI rate?
check.a: About half a bar width nose-down [[23:165|IFH 7-4]], for a descent near 120 fpm, double the error [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].

body.p: The POH gives the climb airspeed and power. For a given power and load there is only one attitude for the most efficient climb [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].

head: Step
Constant-airspeed climb
Constant-rate climb or descent
rows: Raise the miniature airplane to the climb attitude. Add climb power with the pitch change, or as airspeed nears climb speed [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]
Set power for the rate and the attitude together. Airspeed is primary for pitch until the VSI nears the target [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]
Airspeed primary for pitch; tach or manifold pressure primary for power [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]
VSI primary for pitch; airspeed primary for power [[23:175|IFH 7-14]] [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]
Airspeed low or high: small pitch change [[23:175|IFH 7-14]]
Vertical speed right but airspeed low: add power and lower the nose slightly [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]

body.p: **Descents.** First slow to descent airspeed in level flight. Then reduce power to a set value, lower the nose to hold airspeed, and trim. This works with or without the attitude indicator [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

head: Level-off
Lead
Then
rows: 10 percent of the vertical speed: 500 fpm, 50 ft; 1,000 fpm, 100 ft [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]
To level at cruise: lower the nose, keep climb power until near cruise speed, then reduce [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]
From a 500 fpm descent, speeding up
Add cruise power at the lead point and hold forward pressure so the nose doesn't rise. Ease to level about 50 ft above [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]
From a descent, staying at descent speed
Level the nose and add power to hold the airspeed [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]

callout.text: Ballooning on a level-off from a descent comes from not holding the descent attitude with forward pressure as you add power [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

check.q: You are climbing at 800 fpm toward 6,000 ft. When do you start the level-off?
check.a: At about 5,920 ft. Ten percent of 800 fpm is an 80-foot lead [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

chunks.title: Turns: standard rate, timed and compass

body.p: A standard-rate turn is 3° per second, a full 360° in 2 minutes. A faster airplane needs more bank for the same rate [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

callout.text: Standard-rate bank is about 15 percent of true airspeed: TAS ÷ 10, plus half that. 100 knots: 10 + 5 = 15°. 120 knots: about 18° [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

bullets: Roll in with coordinated aileron and rudder. Pilots commonly roll in much too fast [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

Set the bank on the attitude indicator, then confirm standard rate on the turn coordinator. Once established, the turn coordinator is primary for bank and the attitude indicator supports [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].
As bank increases, vertical lift decreases. Check the altimeter and VSI and raise the nose slightly. Airspeed is primary for power; add power as drag rises [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].
Roll out at the same rate you rolled in. Lead the heading by half your bank: with 10° of bank, start 5° early [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].
For small heading changes, bank no more than the number of degrees to turn [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

body.p: **Timed turns** use the clock and turn coordinator. At standard rate you turn 45° in 15 seconds; at half standard rate, 45° takes 30 seconds. Start rolling in as the second hand passes a cardinal point, and roll out when the computed time is up [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. Calibrate the turn coordinator first: at standard rate the heading should change 30° every 10 seconds [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].
**Compass turns.** With 15° to 18° of bank, the lead or lag for turns to north or south is about equal to your latitude [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].

head: Turning to
Start the roll-out (IFH example: 30° latitude, 15° bank)
rows: Compass reads 037: latitude plus half the bank, before north [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]
Compass reads 203: 180 + 30, minus half the bank [[23:183|IFH 7-22]]
East or west, from a northerly heading
East or west, from a southerly heading

check.q: In a timed turn, how long does a 90° heading change take at standard rate?

body.p: Gyro instruments run on separate electric or vacuum (pneumatic) sources, so a single failure should not take away everything [[23:112|IFH 5-17]]. Many airplanes run the attitude indicator on vacuum and the turn indicator on electricity, or the reverse. Check the POH/AFM so you know what fails together [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].

head: Problem
What you see
rows: Attitude and heading indicator gyros slow down and precess (drift). Some airplanes have a low-vacuum light; others only a suction gauge [[1:224|PHAK 8-22]]
Up to 5 minutes, normally 2 to 3, before the attitude indicator is upright [[23:114|IFH 5-19]]
Pitot tube blocked, drain hole open
Pitot tube and drain hole both blocked
Airspeed acts like an altimeter: it rises in a climb and falls in a descent [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]
Altimeter freezes and VSI shows zero. Airspeed reads low above the blockage altitude and high below it [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]
Altimeter slightly high, airspeed high, VSI shows a brief climb [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]
Attitude and heading disappear from the PFD, and unusual-attitude protection is lost [[23:217|IFH 7-56]]
Reversionary mode: flight and engine data shown together on the remaining screen [[23:329|IFH 11-4]]

body.p: Errors in the airspeed indicator and VSI almost always mean a blocked pitot tube, static port, or both. Ice, moisture, dirt or insects can do it, so remove the pitot cover and check the static ports on preflight [[23:97|IFH 5-2]].

callout.text: Airplane or instrument? Any rate of movement or reading that doesn't fit the maneuver: assume an unusual attitude and speed up the cross-check to confirm the attitude, an instrument error or a malfunction [[23:188|IFH 7-27]]. Compare instruments that show the same thing. If the heading keeps changing while the attitude indicator shows wings level and the ball is centered, the airplane is turning and the attitude gyro has precessed [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

body.p: Glass panels have backup instruments that need no electrical power or have their own battery [[23:149|IFH 6-16]]. Keep them in your scan so you can catch a failure in the main system [[23:161|IFH 6-28]].

check.q: In a steady climb the altimeter stops moving and the VSI goes to zero, while the attitude indicator still shows a climb. What is the likely cause?
check.a: Blocked static ports. Trapped static pressure freezes the altimeter and zeroes the VSI [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]. Use the alternate static source if the airplane has one [[23:98|IFH 5-3]].

chunks.title: Partial panel: flying without the attitude and heading gyros

body.p: Every basic maneuver here, except the instrument takeoff, can be flown partial panel, with the attitude indicator and heading indicator covered or inoperative [[23:162|IFH 7-1]]. If you know how to use each instrument by itself, a failure changes little [[23:197|IFH 7-36]].

head: Control
Use instead
rows: Altimeter, VSI and airspeed. How fast the altimeter needle moves tells you how big the pitch error is [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]
Turn coordinator for wings level and standard rate, with the ball centered [[23:168|IFH 7-7]] [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]
Magnetic compass, read in straight, unaccelerated flight; timed turns with the clock [[23:182|IFH 7-21]] [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]
Airspeed and the power instruments, as usual [[23:137|IFH 6-4]]

bullets: Make only small, smooth inputs. Abrupt reactions to altitude changes cause bigger swings and can leave you disoriented [[23:197|IFH 7-36]].
Fixating on the altimeter can cost you heading and airspeed control [[23:197|IFH 7-36]].
Climb entries are easier and more accurate on partial panel if you first slow to climb speed [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].
In a partial panel descent, airspeed, altimeter and VSI show changing rates until the airplane settles at a constant speed, so cross-check carefully [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].
To trim with only the turn coordinator: level its miniature airplane with aileron, center the ball with rudder, then trim the pressures off [[23:169|IFH 7-8]].

callout.text: In the IFH glass example, an AHRS failure removes attitude, heading and the slip/skid indicator from the PFD. With no standby turn coordinator, the compass is left, and it is less useful [[23:217|IFH 7-56]].

check.q: Your vacuum pump fails in the clouds. What do you use for bank and for heading changes?
check.a: The turn coordinator for bank (if it is electric, check the POH) [[23:114|IFH 5-19]], timed turns with the clock, and the compass for headings [[23:182|IFH 7-21]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: the checkride maneuvers

body.p: The examiner watches your cross-check and corrections in straight and level flight, climbs, descents and turns, and holds you to these limits:

bullets: 1. Know the pitch attitude and power setting for each maneuver in your airplane, from the POH/AFM and practice [[23:162|IFH 7-1]] [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].
2. Establish: set pitch and bank on the attitude indicator and set the power [[23:152|IFH 6-19]].
3. Trim off the control pressures [[23:153|IFH 6-20]].
4. Cross-check the primary instruments for the maneuver and the supporting ones that warn of a trend [[23:167|IFH 7-6]].
5. Adjust in small amounts. Don't slow the scan while you wait for the new attitude to settle; keep checking and trimming [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].
6. Lead every level-off and roll-out: 10 percent of the vertical speed, half the bank angle [[23:177|IFH 7-16]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].
7. After a roll-out or level-off, go right back to a fast straight-and-level cross-check [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

callout.text: Fix small errors right away. A 1° heading error takes much less time and attention than a 20° error [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]. If you tolerate any deviation, errors grow [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

check.q: You are 70 ft low, still inside the ±100 ft ACS limit. Do you correct now?
check.a: Yes. Late pitch corrections are a common error; if any deviation is tolerated, errors increase [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

chunks.title: Risk: your body, illusions and the cross-check

body.p: Spatial disorientation means not knowing the airplane's position, attitude or movement. Your brain blends three systems: the inner ear (vestibular), nerves in the skin, muscles and joints, and your eyes [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]]. In clouds the eyes lose the horizon, and false sensations can disorient you fast [[23:70|IFH 3-3]].
In a long, constant turn the inner-ear fluid catches up with the canal, and you feel no turn at all. When you roll out, you feel a turn the other way [[23:72|IFH 3-5]].

head: Illusion
What happens
Trap
rows: An abrupt correction of a bank you entered too slowly to notice feels like a bank the other way [[23:72|IFH 3-5]]
Rolling back into the original bank
A head movement in a long turn feels like rotation on a different axis [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]
The AIM calls it the most overwhelming illusion [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]
In a long turn you feel level but see altitude loss [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]
Fast acceleration feels nose-up; fast deceleration feels nose-down [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]
Pushing into a dive, or pulling toward a stall
An abrupt change from climb to level feels like tumbling backward [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]
An updraft feels like a climb; a downdraft feels like a descent [[23:73|IFH 3-6]] [[23:74|IFH 3-7]]
Sloping clouds or patterns of ground lights look like the horizon [[23:74|IFH 3-7]]
A light you stare at in the dark seems to move [[23:74|IFH 3-7]]

body.p: **Fighting it.** Disorientation can be prevented only by outside reference to fixed points on the ground or by the flight instruments [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]. Use a scan with little head movement, and pick up dropped items carefully [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. Trust the instruments and disregard your sensations [[23:76|IFH 3-9]].

**Physiology degrades the scan.** Illness, medication, alcohol, fatigue, sleep loss and mild hypoxia make you more open to disorientation [[23:75|IFH 3-8]] [[23:76|IFH 3-9]]. Hypoxia narrows your vision and makes instrument interpretation hard, while you feel that all is normal [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]. Skill fatigue makes you focus on the center of your vision and neglect the edges, with less smooth control [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]. That is a broken cross-check.

callout.text: IMSAFE before every flight: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion. Alcohol also makes you more prone to disorientation and hypoxia [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]].

body.p: **Optical illusions** matter most at the end of an approach, when you look outside to land. A narrow runway, upsloping terrain, featureless terrain or rain on the windscreen can make you fly a low approach. Haze can make you low, and fog can feel like pitching up [[23:76|IFH 3-9]]. Check the altimeter often and use VASI, PAPI or a glideslope when you have one [[23:76|IFH 3-9]].

check.q: In a long turn in the clouds you bend down to pick up a dropped pen and suddenly feel the airplane tumbling. What is it, and what do you do?
check.a: The Coriolis illusion. Bring your head back up, fly by the instruments and ignore the sensation, and keep head movement small from now on [[23:73|IFH 3-6]] [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]].

body.p: Instrument techniques change with airplane type, performance and instruments. Study the POH/AFM procedures, performance data and limits before you practice [[23:162|IFH 7-1]].

bullets: Know the airplane's systems, limits and procedures before you fly, with special attention to the flight instruments, avionics and navigation equipment, old or new [[57:9|AC 90-109A p 9]].
Learn the power source of every instrument, so you know what fails together [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].
On some glass panels, some performance instruments are on the MFD, off to your right. Adjust your scan to include them [[23:157|IFH 6-24]].
Trend vectors look ahead different times on different systems [[23:159|IFH 6-26]].
Glass-panel pilots tend to drop the standby instruments and compass from the scan. Find them before you need them [[23:161|IFH 6-28]].
Trim wheels differ. Some don't line up with the airplane's axes, and some turn the opposite way from what you expect [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].
Going to a slower or older airplane has challenges too: avionics may be less capable and handling different [[57:52|AC 90-109A App 10 p 2]].

callout.text: You must be fully trained on the avionics you use. Over-reliance on automation has caused accidents, so stay proficient at hand flying in case the automation fails [[57:52|AC 90-109A App 10 p 2]]. Without regular practice, instrument skill starts to erode almost immediately [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

check.q: You have only flown round gauges and want to rent a glass-panel airplane for an IFR trip. What is the safe plan?
check.a: Get trained on that airplane and its avionics first, including its displays, failure modes and standby instruments [[57:9|AC 90-109A p 9]] [[57:52|AC 90-109A App 10 p 2]].

bullets: Overcontrolling pitch, especially on climb entry. Make small pitch changes and wait for the result [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].
Chasing the VSI instead of cross-checking the other pitch instruments [[23:173|IFH 7-12]] [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].
Not correcting small errors, like a 20 ft altitude error [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].
Pushing the nose down for low airspeed when the real cause is low power [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].
Slowing the cross-check while waiting for a new attitude to settle [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].
Correcting heading with too much bank, or turning the wrong way after misreading the heading indicator [[23:174|IFH 7-13]] [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].
Losing altitude on turn entry and gaining it on roll-out, by not adjusting pitch for the change in vertical lift [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].
Reading bank from the turn coordinator without checking the ball [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].
Using trim to fly instead of to relieve pressure, or not trimming after power changes [[23:174|IFH 7-13]] [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].
Not leading the level-off, so you overshoot the altitude [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].
Staring at the compass during a compass-turn roll-out instead of first getting straight and level [[23:187|IFH 7-26]].

callout.text: Which way is shorter? For a heading over 180°, subtract 200 and add 20 to get its reciprocal: 305 becomes 125. For a heading under 180°, add 200 and subtract 20. From 305 to 110, the shortest way is to the right [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

check.q: Why do pilots tend to lose altitude as they roll into a turn?
check.a: Vertical lift decreases as bank increases. Without a small pitch increase, the airplane descends [[23:181|IFH 7-20]] [[23:186|IFH 7-25]].

f1.caption: Figure 7-22. Straight-and-level flight (normal cruising speed).
f1.alt: Six-pack analog panel with manifold pressure and RPM gauges. Orange labels mark the altimeter as primary pitch, the heading indicator as primary bank and the airspeed indicator as primary power. Tan labels mark the attitude indicator as supporting pitch and bank, the turn coordinator as supporting bank, the VSI as supporting pitch and the manifold pressure gauge as supporting power.

f2.caption: Figure 6-17. Radial cross-check.
f2.alt: Analog instrument panel with yellow arrows pointing out from the attitude indicator in the center toward the airspeed indicator, altimeter, turn coordinator, heading indicator and VSI around it, showing the eyes always return to the attitude indicator.

f3.caption: Figure 7-33. Standard rate turn, constant airspeed.
f3.alt: Analog panel in a left standard-rate turn: attitude indicator banked left, turn coordinator on the left standard-rate mark, heading indicator turning. Labels mark the altimeter as primary pitch, the attitude indicator as primary bank initially and supporting pitch, the airspeed indicator as primary power, the turn coordinator as primary bank once the turn is established, and the VSI as supporting pitch.

f4.caption: Figure 3-5. Angular acceleration.
f4.alt: Four drawings of an inner-ear semicircular canal with fluid (endolymph) and a cupula of hairs: no turning, no sensation; start of turn, fluid lags and bends the hairs so you feel the turn; constant-rate turn, fluid catches up and you feel nothing; turn stopped, fluid keeps moving and you feel a turn the opposite way.

f5.caption: Figure 7-18. Skid indication. Figure 7-19. Slip indication.
f5.alt: Top: a turn coordinator banked left with the ball to the right, beside a turn-and-slip needle deflected left with the ball to the right, showing a skid. Bottom: a turn coordinator banked right with the ball to the right, beside a needle deflected right with the ball to the right, showing a slip.

f6.caption: Figure 3-7. Graveyard spiral.
f6.alt: A small airplane's flight path drawn as a tightening red descending spiral ending in a crash, a blue spinning path labeled graveyard spin, and a dashed blue circle labeled correct path showing the level turn the pilot should have flown.

scenario.title: Night IMC, a tired pilot and a failing vacuum pump
scenario.setup: After a 10-hour workday you take off IFR at night in a rented airplane you have flown only twice. You are in the clouds at 6,000 ft on an assigned heading. You notice the heading indicator has drifted 20° from the compass in 10 minutes. The attitude indicator shows a slight left bank, but the turn coordinator shows wings level with the ball centered. Then you spot the suction gauge reading low. Your body says the airplane is straight and level.

questions.q: What is failing, and which instruments can you still trust?
questions.a: Low vacuum lets the gyros slow and precess, so the attitude and heading indicators are unreliable [[1:224|PHAK 8-22]]. Normal apparent drift is only about 15° per hour, so 20° in 10 minutes is a warning sign [[23:115|IFH 5-20]]. The pitot-static instruments (altimeter, airspeed, VSI) and the compass still work, and so does the turn coordinator if it is electric. The POH tells you which instruments run on what [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].

questions.q: How do you hold heading and altitude now?
questions.a: Fly partial panel: turn coordinator and ball for bank, altimeter, VSI and airspeed for pitch, and the compass for heading in straight, steady flight [[23:162|IFH 7-1]] [[23:187|IFH 7-26]]. Make heading changes as timed turns [[23:182|IFH 7-21]], and use only small, smooth inputs [[23:197|IFH 7-36]].

questions.q: As you roll out of a long timed turn, you feel a strong urge to roll the other way. Why, and what do you do?
questions.a: After a long turn the inner-ear fluid keeps moving when you stop turning, so you feel a turn the opposite way [[23:72|IFH 3-5]]. Believe the turn coordinator and altimeter, not your body [[23:76|IFH 3-9]].

questions.q: A minute later the altimeter is unwinding, airspeed is rising and the turn coordinator shows a left turn, though you feel level. What now?
questions.a: This is the graveyard spiral pattern. Just pulling back tightens the spiral [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]. For a nose-low attitude: reduce power, level the wings with the turn coordinator, then raise the nose smoothly [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

questions.q: How did fatigue and the unfamiliar airplane add to this risk?
questions.a: Fatigue makes disorientation more likely [[23:75|IFH 3-8]] and narrows attention to the center of your vision [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]. With acute fatigue, stay on the ground [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]; IMSAFE would have flagged it [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]]. In an airplane you barely know, you may not know which gyros are vacuum-driven or where to look for the suction gauge. Learn the instruments and avionics before you fly [[57:9|AC 90-109A p 9]].

skills.do: Fly straight and level, climbs, descents and standard-rate turns by instruments, holding altitude ±100 ft in level flight, selected headings ±10°, airspeed ±10 knots and bank ±5° in turns (ACS IR.IV.A.S1).
skills.practice: Fly each maneuver with a full panel, then partial panel, at known pitch and power settings. Use the two-step altitude correction and a VSI rate double the error [[23:165|IFH 7-4]] [[23:166|IFH 7-5]]. Practice airspeed changes in level flight; the IFH calls them an excellent way to build all three basic skills [[23:172|IFH 7-11]].

skills.do: Show a proper cross-check and correct interpretation, and make the right pitch, bank, power and trim corrections (ACS IR.IV.A.S2).
skills.practice: Say out loud the primary instruments for each maneuver and what you will check during each turn [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. Calibrate the turn coordinator and practice timed turns [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. Trim after every change in attitude, power or configuration [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

quiz.q: In the control and performance method, which instruments are the control instruments?
quiz.why: Control instruments show attitude and power: the attitude indicator plus manifold pressure, tachometer or fuel flow. The altimeter, airspeed and VSI are performance instruments [[23:135|IFH 6-2]].

quiz.q: In straight-and-level flight at a constant airspeed, which instrument is primary for pitch?
quiz.why: The altimeter gives the most pertinent altitude information and is primary for pitch. The heading indicator is primary bank and the airspeed indicator primary power [[23:143|IFH 6-10]].

quiz.q: With a selected radial cross-check, about how much of the time are your eyes on the attitude indicator?
quiz.why: You spend 80 to 90 percent of the time on the attitude indicator, with quick glances at the other instruments [[23:144|IFH 6-11]].

quiz.q: You roll out of a 180° steep turn using only the attitude indicator and don't notice a slow heading change. Which cross-check error is this?
quiz.why: Leaving the heading indicator out of the scan after the roll-out is omission. The precessed attitude gyro showed a slight error that a quick look at the other instruments would have caught [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].

quiz.q: You are 100 ft below your assigned altitude. Using the IFH rule of thumb, what vertical speed should you use to return?
quiz.why: Use a rate about double the error: 100 ft off, about 200 fpm [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].

quiz.q: In level cruise you are 80 ft high and 8 knots slow. What is the best correction?
options: Lower the nose slightly, with no power change
Raise the nose and add power
quiz.why: When altitude is high and airspeed is low, a pitch change alone may return both to the desired values [[23:170|IFH 7-9]].

quiz.q: About what bank angle gives a standard-rate turn at 120 knots true airspeed?
quiz.why: Use about 15 percent of TAS: 120 ÷ 10 = 12, plus half (6) = 18° [[23:181|IFH 7-20]].

quiz.q: You are climbing at 700 fpm. How far before your target altitude should you start to level off?
quiz.why: Lead the altitude by 10 percent of the vertical speed: 10 percent of 700 fpm is 70 ft [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

quiz.q: Ice blocks the static ports in cruise and you then start a descent. What do the altimeter and VSI show?
options: Altimeter stuck at the blockage altitude; VSI at zero
Altimeter reads high; VSI shows a climb
Altimeter unwinds faster than normal; VSI pegged down
quiz.why: Trapped static pressure freezes the altimeter at the altitude where the blockage happened, and the VSI shows a continuous zero [[23:98|IFH 5-3]].

quiz.q: Just after takeoff into a low overcast you accelerate quickly and feel as if the nose is pitching up steeply. What is the illusion, and what is the danger?
options: Elevator illusion; you may climb too steeply
Somatogravic illusion; you may push into a nose-low attitude
Coriolis illusion; you may roll into a bank
quiz.why: Rapid acceleration stimulates the otolith organs like tilting the head back. The disoriented pilot may push into a nose-low or dive attitude [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

takeaways: Attitude plus power equals performance: establish, trim, cross-check, adjust.
Primary is the instrument that tells you most for the maneuver. Level flight: altimeter for pitch, heading indicator for bank, airspeed for power.
Scan through the attitude indicator, and watch for fixation, omission and emphasis.
Small corrections: half a bar under 100 ft, a VSI rate double the error, bank no more than the degrees to turn.
Lead level-offs by 10 percent of the vertical speed and roll-outs by half the bank. Standard-rate bank is about TAS ÷ 10 plus half.
Know what powers each gyro, spot failures by comparing instruments, and fly partial panel with small inputs.
Trust the instruments, not your body, and run IMSAFE before you go.
cfi_notes: The IFH is inconsistent on the overcontrolling rule. IFH 6-6 and 7-37 say more than 200 fpm above the desired rate (500 desired, over 700 is overcontrolling; 400 desired, 600 is overcontrolling), but the example on IFH 7-5 says a 200 ft correction above 400 fpm is overcontrolling. Teach the 6-6 and 7-37 version [[23:139|IFH 6-6]] [[23:198|IFH 7-37]].

The IFH gives two numbers for leaving the heading indicator out of the scan in a 90° standard-rate turn: about 25 seconds on 6-13 and about 20 seconds on 7-25 [[23:146|IFH 6-13]] [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. Either way, the point is to use that time for pitch and power.

IFH 6-28 still refers to the Instrument Rating Practical Test Standards (PTS) [[23:161|IFH 6-28]]. The current standard is the Instrument Rating ACS: ±100 ft, ±10° heading, ±10 knots, ±5° bank (ACS IR.IV.A.S1).

The IFH compass-turn rule (lead or lag about equal to latitude, plus or minus half the bank) differs from the PHAK rule (15° plus half the latitude) [[23:183|IFH 7-22]] [[1:228|PHAK 8-26]]. Pick one for the student and mention the other exists.

Examiners often ask which instrument is primary for pitch in a constant-airspeed climb (airspeed) versus a constant-rate climb (VSI). Have students say the primaries out loud before each maneuver [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].

Demonstrate the disorientation maneuvers only at a safe altitude with an instructor or safety pilot on board [[23:75|IFH 3-8]]. Even no sensation is a useful demonstration, since it shows the body can't detect the bank [[23:74|IFH 3-7]].
Build partial panel habits here; they carry into ACS IR.VII.D, the approach with loss of primary flight instrument indicators.
gaps: Pitch attitudes and power settings for each maneuver in the training airplane come from its POH/AFM and practice; the IFH numbers (23 inches for 120 knots, 18 inches for 100 knots) are only an example.
Failure annunciations, reversionary behavior and standby instrument battery time for a specific PFD or AHRS come from that avionics' AFM supplement; the IFH shows only one example system.
No source gives a set procedure for deciding which of two disagreeing instruments has failed; the lesson uses the IFH advice to speed up the cross-check and compare related instruments.
The ACS also lists the RMH (FAA-H-8083-2) and IPH (FAA-H-8083-16), but neither adds basic attitude-flying content beyond the IFH; the risk material here comes from the IFH, PHAK, AIM and AC 90-109A.

activities.title: Which instrument is primary?
activities.intro: Tap a flight condition, then the instrument that is primary for it.

activities.title: Fixation, omission or emphasis?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: Staring at an altimeter 200 ft low while the heading wanders
Gazing at the manifold pressure gauge during a speed change
Trying to hold the airspeed tape within 1 knot
Never glancing at the standby instruments on a glass panel
Rolling out of a steep turn and never checking heading
Holding altitude with only the attitude indicator
Relying on the one instrument you understand best, even when it is wrong

activities.title: Level off from a climb at cruise speed
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Note your vertical speed and figure a lead of 10 percent of it
At the lead point, smoothly lower the nose toward the level attitude
Watch the VSI move to zero and the altimeter needle slow down
Keep climb power while the airspeed builds
As airspeed nears cruise, reduce power to the cruise setting
Trim and go back to the straight-and-level cross-check

activities.title: True or false: your body in the clouds
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: In a long constant-rate turn, the inner ear can stop sensing the turn at all.
cards.why: True. The fluid catches up with the canal walls and the brain gets the false impression that turning has stopped [[23:72|IFH 3-5]].

cards.s: If you concentrate, your sense of balance will keep you oriented in the clouds.
cards.why: False. Disorientation can be prevented only by visual reference to fixed points on the ground or by the flight instruments [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]].

cards.s: Pulling back when you see altitude loss in an unnoticed turn can tighten a graveyard spiral.
cards.why: True. The disoriented pilot pulls back, tightening the spiral and losing more altitude [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]].

cards.s: A rapid acceleration on takeoff can feel like a nose-down attitude.
cards.why: False. It feels nose-up (somatogravic illusion), and the pilot may push into a dive [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

cards.s: Fatigue, alcohol and mild hypoxia make spatial disorientation more likely.
cards.why: True. Illness, medication, alcohol, fatigue, sleep loss and mild hypoxia increase susceptibility [[23:75|IFH 3-8]] [[23:76|IFH 3-9]].

cards.s: Hypoxia always gives a clear warning before your instrument scan suffers.
cards.why: False. Hypoxia makes instrument interpretation difficult and can give you a false sense that everything is normal [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].

cards.s: Rain on the windscreen can make you feel higher than you are, so you fly a low approach.
cards.why: True. The horizon appears lower than it is, which can lead to a lower approach [[23:76|IFH 3-9]].

final_quiz.q: You want a turn of 3° per second at a TAS of 140 knots. Using the IFH rule of thumb, how much bank do you roll into?
final_quiz.why: TAS ÷ 10 = 14, plus half of that (7) = 21°, about 15 percent of TAS [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:181|IFH 7-20]]. 14° forgets to add the half.

final_quiz.q: With the heading indicator failed, you need to turn right from 030° to 165° at standard rate. How long do you hold the turn?
final_quiz.why: 135° of turn at 3° per second is 45 seconds [[23:182|IFH 7-21]]. 90 seconds would be a half-standard-rate turn.

final_quiz.q: You are 250 ft high and start back down. Using the IFH rules of thumb, what VSI reading would show you are overcontrolling?
final_quiz.why: The desired rate is double the error, 500 fpm. More than 200 fpm above the desired rate, so over 700 fpm, is overcontrolling [[23:139|IFH 6-6]] [[23:198|IFH 7-37]].

final_quiz.q: You are on a heading of 305° and ATC assigns 110°. Which way is the shortest turn, and about how far?
final_quiz.why: The reciprocal of 305 is 125 (subtract 200, add 20), so 110 lies to the right [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. Right: 305 to 360 is 55°, plus 110 is 165°.

final_quiz.q: Your vacuum pump fails. The turn coordinator is electric. Which group of instruments can you still trust?
options: Altimeter, airspeed, VSI, compass and turn coordinator
final_quiz.why: Low vacuum makes the attitude and heading gyros slow and precess [[1:224|PHAK 8-22]]. Pitot-static instruments, the compass and an electrically powered turn instrument are not vacuum-driven; the POH tells you each instrument's power source [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].

final_quiz.q: Using only the magnetic compass near 40° N latitude with a 16° bank, you turn left from east to north. Using the IFH rule, when do you start the roll-out?
final_quiz.why: Turning to north, lead by the latitude plus your normal roll-out lead (half the bank): 40 + 8 = 48°, so start at 048 [[23:183|IFH 7-22]].

final_quiz.q: Your PFD's altitude trend vector shows where you will be in 6 seconds. You pass 4,400 ft climbing at 1,200 fpm. Where does the trend vector point?
final_quiz.why: 1,200 fpm ÷ 60 = 20 ft per second; 20 × 6 = 120 ft; 4,400 + 120 = 4,520 ft, the same method as the IFH example [[23:159|IFH 6-26]].

final_quiz.q: After a turn, the attitude indicator shows wings level and the ball is centered, but the heading indicator keeps slowly turning. What is going on?
options: The airplane is turning and the attitude gyro has precessed
The compass needs to be reset
final_quiz.why: If the heading changes while the attitude indicator shows level and the ball is centered, the attitude gyro has precessed. Stop the heading change and retrim [[23:186|IFH 7-25]]. A skid would show the ball off center.

final_quiz.q: You suspect a blocked static port and open the alternate static source inside the cabin. What changes should you expect?
options: Altimeter slightly low and airspeed low
Altimeter frozen and VSI at zero
Altimeter slightly high, airspeed high, brief climb on the VSI
final_quiz.why: Cabin pressure is lower than outside, so the altimeter reads slightly high, airspeed reads high and the VSI shows a momentary climb [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]. A frozen altimeter is the sign of the blockage itself.

final_quiz.q: At night in the clouds after a long left turn, you feel level, but the altimeter is unwinding, airspeed is rising and the turn coordinator shows a left turn. What should you do?
options: Pull back firmly to stop the descent
Reduce power, level the wings with the turn coordinator, then raise the nose
Roll right until your body feels level
final_quiz.why: This is the graveyard spiral pattern; pulling back tightens it [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]. For a nose-low attitude, reduce power, level the wings by the turn coordinator, then raise the nose [[23:189|IFH 7-28]].

final_quiz.q: You have flown only analog panels and want to rent a glass-panel airplane for an IFR trip next week. What is the best way to manage the risk?
options: Fly it IFR and learn the displays en route
Rely on the autopilot so the new displays matter less
Skip the standby instruments, since glass rarely fails
Get training on that airplane and its avionics, including failures and standby instruments
final_quiz.why: Know the systems, avionics and procedures before you fly, and be fully trained on the equipment [[57:9|AC 90-109A p 9]] [[57:52|AC 90-109A App 10 p 2]]. Over-reliance on automation has caused accidents, and glass pilots often omit the standby instruments [[23:161|IFH 6-28]].

final_quiz.q: Late in a long duty day, you notice you are watching only the attitude indicator and missing the other instruments, and your control is getting rough. What effect of skill fatigue does this match?
final_quiz.why: Disruption of the perceptual field means focusing on the center of vision and neglecting the periphery, with less accurate and smooth control [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]. Timing disruption is when each part of a task is done as if separate.

final_quiz.q: You are descending at 500 fpm and want to level at 4,000 ft and speed up to cruise. When do you add cruise power?
final_quiz.why: At 500 fpm, lead the altitude by 100 to 150 ft when leveling at a speed higher than descent speed, and add cruise power at the lead point [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. The 50 ft lead is for leveling at descent speed.

final_quiz.q: In level flight at cruise power, both your altitude and your airspeed are below what you want. What correction do you make?
options: Raise the nose and add power
final_quiz.why: When altitude and airspeed are both low (or both high), you need a change in both pitch and power [[23:170|IFH 7-9]].
